See same source, p. 270. Other later Islamic philosophers already mentioned—note 31 of this chapter—also report Abū Bakr al-Rāzī’s doctrine of the eternity of space and time in roughly the same form as Nāṣir-i Khusraw. They include al-Marzūqī, Ibn Ḥazm, al-Kātibī, and Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī. See Kraus, same source, pp. 241–242. Abū Bakr al-Rāzī himself says in The Philosophical Life that he wrote a treatise “On Time, Space, Duration, Eternity, and the Void.” Like so many of his other works, this treatise has not reached us. Everything we say about his philosophical doctrine therefore comes through authors who present it briefly and in fragments. We do not know how much their abbreviated and piecemeal reports may have altered its real substance.↩︎
See al-Qifṭī, Accounts of the Sages, p. 271.↩︎
In medieval Arabic philosophical literature and histories of Arabic philosophy, “the ancients” means the ancient Greek philosophers. See al-Shahrastānī, Religions and Sects, vol. 2, p. 94.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā is not known to have written in any language other than Arabic except for a treatise on the principles of the sciences dedicated to ʿAlāʾ al-Dawla ibn Kākawayh, who seized Hamadan and Isfahan in 414 AH under the Buyids and for whom Ibn Sīnā later served as vizier, and a second short treatise on “pulses.” Both were written in Persian. He also wrote a Treatise on the Philosophy of Death for his brother, of which a Persian copy exists in the British Museum. See Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, trans. ʿĀdil Zuʿaytir, p. 149. As for his poetry, no biographer or cataloguer of his works says that he composed anything in Persian beyond a few poems and quatrains totaling no more than sixty-five verses. All the rest of his poetry is in Arabic. See Aḥmad Fuʾād al-Ahwānī, Ibn Sīnā, Cairo, no date, p. 38.↩︎

While dictating the story of his early life to his student al-Jūzjānī, Ibn Sīnā said: “My father was one of those who answered the call of the Egyptians [the Fatimids] and was counted among the Ismāʿīlīs, as was my brother. The two of them would sometimes discuss these matters with each other while I listened and understood what they were saying, and they began to invite me to it as well....” See al-Qifṭī, Accounts of the Sages, p. 269.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā served twice as vizier to the Buyid ruler Shams al-Dawla in Hamadan. Between the two periods, the troops rebelled against him, surrounded his house, arrested him, and demanded that the ruler have him killed because they feared he would punish them for their misconduct. Ibn Sīnā went into hiding for forty days. Shams al-Dawla then called him back to treat him medically and restored him to the vizierate. See previously cited source. It is also said that ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ibn Kākawayh, ruler of Isfahan, made him his vizier. See al-Ahwānī, Ibn Sīnā, p. 10.↩︎
He is said to have written The Salvation while traveling with ʿAlāʾ al-Dawla to Sābūrkhwāst. See Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, p. 140.↩︎
Al-Jūzjānī says in his biography of Ibn Sīnā: “Teaching took place at night because during the day he had no free time from serving the ruler.” Al-Qifṭī, p. 271.↩︎

Al-Jūzjānī says: “During this period”—that is, during Ibn Sīnā’s service as vizier to Shams al-Dawla—“students of learning gathered every night in the house of the Supreme Master. After the reading was finished, singers of different kinds would arrive and the drinking session would begin....” Al-Qifṭī, previously cited source.↩︎

Al-Jūzjānī also says: “After Shams al-Dawla died, his son was recognized as ruler, but the Shaykh refused to become his vizier and secretly asked ʿAlāʾ al-Dawla to take him into his service. When the ruler learned of this, he imprisoned him in the fortress of Fardajān, where he remained for four months.” Same source. Henry Corbin says that Ibn Sīnā wrote his Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān during this period of imprisonment in the fortress (p. 257).↩︎
Ibn Sīnā, The Adḥawiyya Treatise on the Afterlife, Cairo, 1949, ed. Sulaymān Dunyā, p. 112.↩︎
Ibn Sīnā says in his autobiography: “My father then began sending me to a man who sold vegetables and knew Indian arithmetic, so that I could learn from him.” See al-Qifṭī, p. 269.↩︎
Ibn Sīnā’s social views appear in the final chapters of the tenth treatise in the metaphysics section of The Healing.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā says in his autobiography: “The ruler of Bukhara at that time was Nūḥ ibn Manṣūr. He fell ill with a disease that baffled the physicians. By then my name had become known among them because of the intensity of my study. They mentioned me to him and asked that I be brought in. I came and joined them in treating him, and I entered his service. One day I asked him for permission to enter their library...” and so on. Al-Qifṭī, previously cited source.↩︎

In his biography of Ibn Sīnā, Abū ʿUbayd al-Jūzjānī says that Ibn Sīnā’s connection with “the Lady,” the mother of Majd al-Dawla, began because her son suffered from melancholy, and Ibn Sīnā treated him. Shams al-Dawla later called on Ibn Sīnā to treat him for colic, described here as an ulcerative disease of the stomach. Ibn Sīnā’s return to the vizierate under Shams al-Dawla was also connected with this illness. It returned after Ibn Sīnā had gone into hiding following the soldiers’ rebellion against him, forcing Shams al-Dawla to summon him for treatment. Shams al-Dawla apologized to him and then restored him to the vizierate. See al-Qifṭī, previously cited source.↩︎

We have decisive evidence for this in Ibn Sīnā’s own account of his life: “I attended to the sick, and doors of treatment based on experience opened to me beyond description.” His student al-Jūzjānī continues: “The Shaykh accumulated many experiences from the treatments he personally carried out, and intended to record them in The Canon. He had written them down on separate sheets, but they were lost before The Canon was completed.” Al-Jūzjānī then gives us a concrete example of Ibn Sīnā’s experimental method: “One day he developed a headache. He ordered a large quantity of ice to be brought, crushed, wrapped in a cloth, and placed over his head. This was done until the area was strengthened and could no longer receive the offending matter, and he recovered. In another case, a woman with tuberculosis in Khwarazm was ordered to take no medicine except sugared julanjubīn [a paste made from roses and honey] until, over time, she had consumed one hundred mann”—an old measure here estimated at about 25 kilograms—“and the woman recovered.” See al-Qifṭī, previously cited source.↩︎

Among the best-known representatives of this doctrine in modern philosophy are Francis Bacon (1561–1626) and John Locke (1632–1704) among the materialists, and George Berkeley (1685–1753) and David Hume (1711–1776) among the idealists. In Dialectics of Nature, Engels says that Bacon’s empiricism became the starting point of modern metaphysics, which separates phenomena from one another without attending to the connections between them. Locke, for his part, recognized only the essences of individual things and rejected the idea of a general essence.↩︎

There is abundant evidence for this in Ibn Sīnā, and it shows that sensory knowledge must rely on reasoning, while reasoning must also rely on sensory knowledge. In The Salvation (p. 65), for example, he says that the senses grasp particulars, while rational thought reaches abstract universals. In the chapter on sensory data (The Salvation, p. 61), he says that matters established by experience—meaning sensory experience—are propositions to which the senses lead us with the help of reasoning. In defining induction, he says that it is “a judgment about a universal because that judgment is found in the particulars belonging to that universal, either in all of them, which is complete induction, or in most of them, which is the commonly used form of induction” (The Salvation, p. 58). See also Pointers and Reminders, vol. 3, pp. 17–19, where Ibn Sīnā answers those who claim that only what can be sensed truly exists.↩︎

In Ibn Sīnā’s logical terminology, “accident,” “inseparable attribute,” and “concomitant” refer to conditions connected with the actual existence of things—that is, with the existence of the individual or particular thing.↩︎
In logical terminology, a “description” (rasm) defines a thing through the properties of its actual existence—its accidents, inseparable attributes, and concomitants.↩︎

It is useful here to state the position of dialectical materialism on logic as Lenin summarized it: “Logic is not the doctrine of the external forms of thought, but the doctrine of the laws governing the development of all material, natural, and spiritual things—that is, the development of the whole concrete content of the world and of our knowledge of it. In other words, it is the sum of the conclusions drawn from the history of human knowledge of the world.” Lenin, Collected Works, vol. 29, p. 84, Russian ed.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā uses this name in States of the Soul, p. 61, and in The Salvation, p. 163. In Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, p. 353, he writes it as bifṭāsiyā. The word is Greek in origin: phantasia. Aristotle used it in the sense of imagination and says that the word is derived from “light” (phaos). See Aristotle, On the Soul, Arabic ed., trans. al-Ahwānī, 2nd ed., Cairo, 1962, p. 107. Here Aristotle and Ibn Sīnā differ both in terminology and in substance. Aristotle uses phantasia for the imaginative faculty and treats it as the second stage in the process of thinking, with common sense as the first. Ibn Sīnā, by contrast, applies phantasia to common sense itself, even though he explains the word as meaning imagination. They also differ in how they explain common sense. Ibn Sīnā says that it is the faculty that receives all the forms impressed upon the senses. Aristotle says that common sense perceives motion, rest, shape, magnitude, number, and unity—things that no single sense perceives on its own. See same source, pp. 93–101.↩︎

The Salvation, p. 163, and States of the Soul, p. 61. In Pointers and Reminders (vol. 2, p. 353), Ibn Sīnā says that the organ of common sense is “the spirit poured into the beginnings of the sensory nerves.” In The Salvation and States of the Soul on the pages just cited, however, he says that this faculty is “located in the first cavity of the brain.”↩︎
